name: Libertarian Paternalism
description: The position that choice architects can and should steer people's decisions toward outcomes that improve their own welfare, while preserving each person's freedom to choose otherwise -- the foundational philosophical framework behind 'nudge' interventions.
design_relevance_note: The philosophical justification underlying every 'good' nudge in this corpus's Choice Architecture cluster -- a direct test for whether a given design intervention (a default setting, a suggested option, a framing choice) genuinely preserves the user's ability to choose otherwise, or has quietly become coercive despite being labeled a nudge.
myth_risk_note: The framework itself is philosophically well-argued and foundational, but 'libertarian paternalism' is sometimes invoked to justify an intervention (a sticky default, a hard-to-find opt-out) without independently checking whether the choice to opt out is genuinely as easy as the framework requires -- the label itself is not evidence that a specific real-world application meets its own stated bar. Raised from low to moderate 2026-09-10 after adding Gigerenzer (2015)'s well-cited, direct dispute of the framework's own core evidentiary justification -- the philosophical framework itself isn't in question, but the specific 'people are hardly educable' premise commonly cited to justify choosing intervention over education now has a real, live academic challenge on file, not just uncontested self-justification.
prevalence_note: The philosophical foundation for the entire behavioral-economics 'nudge' movement and this corpus's whole Choice Architecture & Value Framing cluster -- extremely well known by name in policy and behavioral-design circles, even though the term itself (as opposed to 'nudge') is used more in academic/policy writing than everyday product-design vocabulary.

findings.description: Directly challenges the evidentiary basis libertarian paternalists (Thaler & Sunstein and others) cite to justify steering people's choices: argues the claim that human reasoning is 'hardly educable' (because cognitive biases supposedly resemble stable visual illusions) rests on narrow logical norms (a mischaracterization of what counts as rational thinking) and a confirmation bias in which research is selectively reported. Concludes the evidence does not support treating people as unable to learn to reason about risk, and that this framing forecloses the alternative of teaching risk literacy directly rather than defaulting to choice-architecture intervention.
findings.source_title: On the Supposed Evidence for Libertarian Paternalism

findings.description: Some form of paternalism in choice architecture is unavoidable (someone must set a default or frame options); this can be done in a way that respects freedom of choice while still steering toward welfare-improving outcomes ('libertarian paternalism').
